A quick post about a phrase that has proven useful in teaching statistics.

```{r}

library(ggplot2) # dummy call to ggplot

```

```{css, echo = FALSE}

.math.display .MathJax {
  font-size: 300% !important;
}

```

$$\text{\color{purple}{Data}} = \text{\color{blue}{Model}} + \text{\color{red}{Error}}$$ {#eq-data-equals-model-plus-error}

I have no clear memory of where I first heard this phrase, but I have an idea that it was in the blog of [https://www.johndcook.com/](https://www.johndcook.com/).

The idea, as I have understood it, is that our [**observed data about the real world**]{fg="#800080"}, can be broken down into two parts: [**our model of the world**]{fg="#0000FF"}; and [**the ways in which our model is wrong**]{fg="#FF0000"}.

Consider a basic regression equation:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + e_i$$

Broadly speaking, as we add independent variables (e.g. $x_2, x_3, \text{etc}...$) to the [**model**]{fg="#0000FF"} we reduce the amount of variation in $y_i$ that needs to be explained by the [**error**]{fg="#FF0000"}, $e_i$:  as the model gains more power, the error decreases
